analysis.title: Weekly Economics: Strong But Concentrated Economic Growth (October 30, 2026)
key_insights: 3Q26 real GDP rose 3.4% quarter-over-quarter, seasonally adjusted annualized, in line with the report's own 3.5% forecast. Consumer spending and AI and data center investment were the main drivers.
Real gross private domestic investment rose 19.4% in 3Q26 after 4.6% in 2Q26. Nonresidential investment rose 12.7% and equipment investment rose 20.9%. Residential investment fell 3.3%.

Contributions to 3Q26 GDP growth: personal consumption 2.52 pp, gross private domestic investment 3.27 pp (of which inventories 1.61 pp), government 0.90 pp, net exports -3.32 pp. The authors say a sizable share of AI-related investment is imported, which widens the trade deficit.

Information processing equipment accounted for slightly more than half of 3Q26 real private fixed investment growth. The authors warn that investment growth is becoming dependent on a single segment while other sectors lag.

The conflict with Iran had a larger-than-expected effect on activity. Federal defense spending rose 11.7% and nondefense spending rose 22.2%, so government consumption and investment rose 5.3% after -0.1% in 2Q26.

Bottom line: AI-related spending supports both the economy and markets, but growth is increasingly concentrated. The larger risk is that expectations have moved ahead of the eventual payoff, not weak growth today.

The Fed left rates unchanged in October on a 10-2 vote. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a 25 basis point increase. The report refers to a rate increase in September.

Chairman Warsh said financial conditions have tightened but he is unwilling to call them tight enough for price stability. He said energy prices are too high and are starting to affect other sectors, and that he does not favor forward guidance outside a crisis.
Warsh said the Fed will hold eight meetings a year, but one in 2027 will not involve rate changes. In 2028 there will be 6 policy meetings and 2 strategy meetings with no rate changes.

September PCE prices rose 0.5% month-on-month for headline and 0.3% for core, as expected. Year-over-year, headline accelerated to 3.6% and core to 3.1%. August core was revised up from 0.2% to 0.3%, which the report reads as inflation pressure beyond energy.
3Q26 PCE prices slowed sharply on a quarterly annualized basis, to 2.1% headline and 2.5% core, from 5.0% headline in 2Q26. The authors say this supports the Fed's decision to hold.
September personal income rose 0.2%, and real disposable income fell 0.3% month-on-month. Spending rose 0.5%, and the saving rate fell to 3.8% from 4.0%.
The 3Q26 Employment Cost Index rose 0.8% quarter-over-quarter and 3.4% year-over-year. Wages and salaries rose 3.1% and benefits 3.9%, while real compensation fell 0.6% year-over-year.

September durable goods orders rose 1.8%, in line with expectations. Nondefense capital goods orders rose 6.2% and nondefense aircraft orders rose 28.4%. Defense capital goods orders fell 1.8%, the third straight monthly decline. The report says capital goods orders continue to point to strong AI and data center investment.

October Consumer Confidence rose 7.5 points to 91.7, well above the 80.5 consensus, helped by softer gasoline prices. The index remains on a downtrend since 2022, and consumers planned less spending on services and durables.
FHFA home prices rose 0.3% in August and 2.4% year-over-year, despite higher mortgage rates. The report says this further reduces affordability.

September new home sales ran at 676,000 annualized, which the report calls stronger than expected. Supply stood at 8.4 months, and the median price was $400,400. The authors expect residential investment to remain a drag on GDP in 3Q and 4Q 2026.

risk_factors: Growth is concentrated in AI and data center investment, and expectations may be ahead of the eventual payoff.
A reversal in investor caution could weaken investment, which is more volatile than consumption.
A large share of AI-related investment is imported, so net exports subtracted 3.32 pp from 3Q26 GDP growth.
Inflation remains elevated, with PCE at 3.6% and core at 3.1% year-over-year, and the Fed has two dissenters favoring a hike.
Real disposable income fell 0.3% in September and the saving rate dropped to 3.8%, which weakens the consumer backbone.
Energy prices are high enough to affect other sectors, per Chairman Warsh.
Residential investment will drag on GDP in 3Q and 4Q 2026.

tension_points.bull_case: AI and data center spending delivers real economic gains and supports market performance. Domestic computer and electronics production is growing at an exceptionally strong pace, and imported capital goods build productive capacity for future output.
tension_points.bear_case: Investment growth depends increasingly on one segment, with information processing equipment supplying slightly more than half of 3Q26 growth. Much of it is imported, and expectations may be ahead of the eventual payoff.
tension_points.what_invalidates: AI-related spending stops expanding, since the report's support for growth and markets holds only as long as that spending continues.

tension_points.bull_case: 3Q26 PCE inflation slowed to 2.1% headline and 2.5% core quarterly annualized, supporting the Fed's decision to hold rates.
tension_points.bear_case: Year-over-year PCE accelerated to 3.6% headline and 3.1% core, August core was revised up, and two FOMC members dissented in favor of a 25 basis point hike.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI investment supports growth and markets, but reliance on one segment raises the risk that expectations outrun the payoff.
Higher prices are eroding wages and consumer purchasing power even as spending holds up.
theme_stances.evidence: the loss in purchasing power of wages and salaries
